analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims and their families sue makers and sellers of untraceable ghost guns.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Ghost guns are firearms without serial numbers, often assembled at home from kits, so they cannot be traced. The bill would let anyone injured or whose family member was killed by a ghost gun, plus the local government where it happened, sue in federal court against whoever made a component of the gun or helped sell it. Courts could award damages, with limited exceptions for lawful self-defense and law enforcement. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by ghost guns, families of those killed by them, and the state and local governments that bear the costs of gun violence; they would gain a new way to recover damages and to hold kit makers and sellers financially accountable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shooting victims, their families, local governments

how_it_helps.text: Anyone injured by a ghost gun, or any family member of someone killed by one, could sue the maker of any component of the gun or any person who facilitated its sale for damages, including consequential damages [S3].
State and local governments where the injury or death occurred could also sue, giving them a way to recover costs tied to ghost gun violence [S3].

The bill defines a ghost gun as a firearm lacking a serial number engraved by a licensed manufacturer or importer, including kits intended to be assembled into such a firearm, so it targets the untraceable weapons used to evade background checks and tracing [S3].

The bill includes an affirmative defense for injuries caused by lawful self-defense or by law enforcement responding to a threat, narrowing the liability to prevent suits against people acting lawfully [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that manufacture ghost gun components and kits, and retailers or online sellers who facilitate ghost gun sales, would face civil lawsuits and damage awards; ghost gun prices could rise as sellers price in the new liability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ghost gun kit makers and sellers

drawbacks.text: Liability would attach to component makers and sellers without requiring proof of any wrongdoing on their part, since the trigger is simply that the gun lacked a serial number and was used to injure someone, which critics would call a form of strict liability [S3].

Determining which component maker or which seller 'facilitated' a sale of a homemade gun assembled from parts could be difficult, inviting litigation against parties with only tenuous connections to the weapon [S3].

A civil-suit approach does not stop ghost gun use before an injury occurs; it compensates victims after the fact rather than preventing shootings, and may overlap with the 2024 federal rule requiring serializations of kit guns, which addresses the problem directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real remedy to a narrow group of victims of an untraceable weapon that is difficult to regulate through conventional background checks, and its self-defense and law-enforcement exceptions show an attempt to avoid abusive suits. The main cost is new litigation exposure for kit makers and sellers, which is precisely the deterrent effect intended. The approach is narrow — it does not require serializing ghost guns or stop their manufacture — but as a victims' compensation tool it is straightforward and modestly designed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2023 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ritchie Torres introduced the bill on June 9, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1].
No further action appears in the record after the referral; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ghost gun kit makers and sellers, who avoided a new civil-liability exposure for two more years, and they bear no risk from the bill's failure; shooting victims and their families gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill creating a civil right of action against ghost gun component makers and sale facilitators.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no vote was ever taken that would show where members stood [S4].

industries.industry: Ghost gun kit manufacturers and sellers
industries.note: The bill would expose them to lawsuits and damage awards whenever their unserialized products are used to injure someone, effectively pricing their liability risk into the cost of kits. Their interest in avoiding suits runs directly against the interest of victims seeking compensation.

The federal Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act shields most gun sellers from suits over criminal misuse of their products; this bill would carve a new liability channel specifically for untraceable firearms, setting a precedent the broader industry would want to resist.
